defect_interactions.interaction_type: DDRX nucleation near original grain boundaries
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Nuclei (small volumes of low dislocation density separated from the matrix by HABs) usually appear near original grain boundaries; several mechanisms such as accelerated rotation of a particular subgrain, coalescence of adjacent subgrains or local migration of a grain boundary are likely. New grains grow at the expense of old hardened grains.

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: At 1100 °C / 10 s−1: LAB : 22%, HAB : 78%, average misorientation angle : 32.9°. A pronounced low-angle peak near 5° (subgrain population intensified relative to 5 s−1); measured distribution is close to the MacKenzie random distribution with a maximum number of HABs near 45°.

interfaces.interface_notes: Black lines = grain boundaries (misorientations θ ≥ 15°); red lines = subgrain boundaries (2° ≤ θ < 15°).
interfaces.phase_evolution: At high temperature and high strain rate (1100 °C, 10 s−1) the alloy undergoes discontinuous dynamic recrystallization (DDRX) instead of continuous dynamic recrystallization (CDRX); there is a competition between the two mechanisms as a function of deformation conditions, with a transition occurring between them.
interfaces.slip_behavior: High stacking fault energy material: cross-slip of dislocations is easy and dynamic recovery is very efficient (relevant to CDRX regime; at 10 s−1 the higher strain rate shortens the test so dynamic recovery is less effective and strain hardening is stronger, enabling DDRX).

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Hot torsion test to a cumulative strain ε = 2 at 1100 °C and strain rate 10 s−1; second of two high strain rate conditions (5 and 10 s−1) examined at 1100 °C to study the DDRX mechanism. Tests were performed in a direction involving a negative shear and under argon atmosphere to reduce oxidation.

After deformation, samples were quenched immediately (0.5 s) with argon in order to retain the microstructures and avoid post-dynamic recrystallization. The cooling rate is ~200 °C s−1 during the first seconds.

structures.overall_structure: DDRX microstructure: a mixture of 'young' small equiaxed freshly recrystallized grains free of substructure and 'old' large elongated original grains displaying internal misorientations (red subgrain boundary lines); a pronounced elongated band with a high density of fine boundaries surrounded by coarse grains. Grain boundaries (HABs, θ ≥ 15°) are dominant (HAB : 78%), with a sharp low-angle (subgrain) peak near 5° (LAB : 22%).

unmapped_findings: At 1100 °C and 10 s−1 (ε = 2), the EBSD maps (Fig. 4b) show a pronounced elongated band containing a high density of fine, red-marked (low-angle) boundaries surrounded by coarse grains, consistent with a changing dynamic-recrystallization mechanism between the 5 and 10 s−1 conditions.

DDRX-produced recrystallized grains have no preferred orientations (very low texture intensity); this is considered a promising result toward decreasing the roping phenomenon, since favouring DDRX during hot rolling yields a microstructure with randomly oriented recrystallized grains (relevant to the Fe–8% Al roping problem).

Although ferritic alloys are high stacking fault energy materials, two types of dynamic recrystallization may operate during hot deformation: DDRX at high temperature and high strain rate and CDRX at lower temperature and strain rate, with a competition between them depending on deformation conditions.

The strain rate–temperature map (Fig. 7) shows the DDRX-activated domain lies above a temperature-dependent threshold strain rate (descending from ~2–3 s−1 at 900 °C to near 0.1–0.2 s−1 at 1100 °C), consistent with DDRX for this 1100 °C, 10 s−1 sample.
